claims.statement: LocalSettingsStore persists one document, AppPaths::resolve(app)?.root.join("settings.json"), where the AppPaths root is Tauri's app_local_data_dir() (Application Support on macOS); it is created in composition.rs and injected as the SettingsPort implementation behind Application.

Settings writes are atomic and private: write_settings creates the parent directory, writes settings.json.part, chmods the temporary to 0600 before renaming, and removes the temporary when the rename fails; a store_settings-level emptiness check (default preset, absent secrets/flags, unset assistant fields, empty roster/glossary) deletes the file instead of writing defaults, so the file's existence means the user changed something.

A settings file that fails JSON parsing surfaces SETTINGS_INVALID to the caller and the corrupt file is left on disk — the store reports rather than resets, so a parse failure cannot destroy the user's roster; the serde(default, camelCase) document also means fields an older build predates load as defaults.

The application layer owns SettingsPort (hugging_face_token_stored, load/save_hugging_face_token, load/save_assistant, load/save_assistant_api_key, load/save_engine_preset); the Tauri commands in adapters/inbound/tauri.rs are thin wrappers over Application, and the TS TauriBackend validates responses with Zod, whose assistantSettingsSchema carries apiKeyStored as a boolean with no field a key value could arrive in.

Never-carry rule: AssistantSettings.api_key_stored is only a flag; save_assistant explicitly writes only model, base_url, reasoning_effort, background, participants, and glossary — never the key — because the sheet autosaves the whole document on any field change and a secret in that payload is one absent field away from being erased; save_assistant_api_key is the key's only entry point, and load_assistant returns the flag without the value.

refine_transcript is the only code path that reads the assistant key (load_assistant_api_key), on the rationale that refinement is the one moment the key is needed and therefore the only moment worth a keychain prompt; a missing key fails with ASSISTANT_KEY_MISSING before any job is claimed.

Both credentials flow through the SecretStore trait (read, write, keeps_plaintext_in_settings): SettingsFile is what production wires — its read/write are no-ops and keeps_plaintext_in_settings() returns true so the secret legitimately lives as a plaintext field in the 0600 settings.json — while Keychain is compiled but unwired, filing items under service com.m16khb.galpi with accounts hugging-face-token / assistant-api-key.

Keychain storage is deferred because macOS ties access to a Keychain item to the code signature that stored it and Galpi's ad-hoc signature changes on every build, so each release would re-prompt every user for a token they never touched; until a stable Developer ID signature exists secrets stay in the settings file, and switching is the one line in LocalSettingsStore::new that constructs SettingsFile.

The Keychain implementation pre-handles the awkward edges: any read failure (absent item or declined access) resolves to None so the caller's own missing-token message wins, and deleting an absent item is success; tests use the InMemorySecrets double, which counts reads and writes so suites can assert a real keychain would have been asked exactly once.

secret() resolves in a fixed order — per-launch cache, then SecretStore, then a legacy plaintext field in the settings document which store_secret migrates — and the cache bounds real keychain access to at most one prompt per secret per launch even though multiple parts of the app request secrets.

Legacy migration keeps the future Keychain switch invisible: a first read of a token still sitting in an older settings.json publishes it through store_secret (user keeps the token without re-entering it), and the plaintext copy is scrubbed from the file when the active store is not the settings file itself (keeps_plaintext_in_settings() false); with today's SettingsFile store the value legitimately stays in the document.

store_secret does nothing at all when the value equals the cached one: because the settings sheet autosaves the whole document on any edit, this no-op keeps an unrelated change (e.g. renaming a participant) from rewriting the API key and re-prompting for keychain authorization; when the value does change it writes the store, updates the cache, and records the *Stored flag while keeping or clearing the plaintext field per keeps_plaintext_in_settings().

secret_stored() answers whether a credential is on file from the settings document's *Stored flag or plaintext presence — keeping merely opening the settings sheet off the keychain; the one exception, an install whose secret was moved before the flag existed, reads the store once and note_secret_present persists the flag so subsequent launches answer from the file.

LocalSettingsStore holds a tokio Mutex across each read-modify-write of the whole document and caches the parsed file: concurrent saves would otherwise each read the same starting state and the second would drop the first's field; a failed write invalidates the cache so the next read re-parses from disk.

The settings sheet has no save button: committed text edits, selects, and roster/glossary row edits trigger AppController's requestSettingsSave, whose single-flight loop (settingsSaveActive/settingsSavePending) coalesces edits made while a write is active into one latest-state write; on failure the sheet preserves edited values, shows a message ending 수정 내용은 유지되며 다음 변경 때 다시 저장합니다., and the next change retries.

Within one autosave, persistSettings sends each credential only when the user actually typed one: TokenSettingsView.pendingToken() and AssistantSettingsView.pendingKey() return null once a credential is stored (the field shows a mask and the window does not hold the value — re-sending is what erased it), so a newly typed value travels on its own saveHuggingFaceToken/saveAssistantApiKey command while the document sent to saveAssistantSettings carries only the apiKeyStored flag; a roster edit therefore never reaches the keychain.

The views keep the window blind to host-held secrets: a stored credential renders as the •••••••••••• mask in a read-only input, persistedToken/persistedKey only ever hold a value the user just typed (never a host-returned one), the visibility toggle is hidden when the window holds nothing revealable, and opening the sheet uses huggingFaceTokenStored plus the flag-carrying loadAssistantSettings without reading any secret; replacing a stored credential is always an explicit clear (empty string, which Application trims and maps to None — a deletion) followed by typing a new value.

The never-carry rule is pinned from both sides: the Rust test an_autosave_cannot_erase_the_stored_assistant_key proves save_assistant leaves a stored key intact in memory and after a simulated relaunch, and settings-autosave.dom.test.ts's 'never rewrites a stored assistant key' test proves an unrelated field edit produces no key writes while apiKeyStored stays true; the DOM suite also covers button-free persistence, newly typed keys on their own command, coalescing, and failure preservation.

Roster value rules live in domain/roster.rs, not the adapter: Application persists settings.trimmed(), where Participant::trimmed drops nameless participants and blank aliases, GlossaryEntry::trimmed drops termless rows and keep_filled turns blanks into None, and reasoning_effort is lowercased and whitelisted to low/medium/high/max (anything else becomes None) — invalid shapes never reach the settings file.

The privacy model is local-first and stated plainly in the README: recording, transcription, alignment, and diarization stay on the Mac, every setting including both credentials is stored in an Application Support settings file with 0600 permissions, and nothing leaves the machine except the AI-augmentation payload (transcript, selected participants, glossary, background context) sent to the configured external API.
